name: Erik Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small worker-owned co-op, eleven of us, that fits solar panels, home batteries and heat pumps. Most days I'm on a roof or in a garage with Femi, our lead electrician, running cable from the panels to the inverter, which is the box that turns the panel power into house power. I'm the junior, so I do the drilling, the clipping, the lifting. In the evenings I'm usually on my laptop asking an AI to explain bits of the wiring rules I didn't get.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that every job cuts someone's bills and their carbon. I'm into all of it, the tech, the batteries, the apps that show a family their power use. What wears me out is that I'm 27 and still making beginner mistakes, like last week I mounted an isolator switch upside down. And winter roofs, those wear anyone out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I use this stuff every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say online that the hype crowd got what they deserved, but that the useful bits are still useful. At the co-op I'd say we keep using it for quotes and design, and move on. Most of my friends would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, and that's okay. The heat pump boom doesn't care whether AI is hype, because people still want lower bills. My job is about as safe as junior jobs get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on my plan: finish my licence next year, then the battery storage certificate. I'd keep putting about 200 a month aside, since we've got about four months saved. And I'd keep using AI to study, because it's helped me more than any textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, maybe, because I was excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI helped you more than a textbook. How exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it things I'd be embarrassed to ask Femi, like why you can't share a neutral between two circuits. It explains it five ways until one clicks. Then I check it against the rule book, because it's wrong maybe one time in twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money situation at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo, my partner, teaches at a primary school, so between us we're fine but not flush. We rent a two-bed above a bakery. The four months saved is mostly Theo's discipline, not mine.

say: I'd say the **useful bits** of AI stay useful even if the hype fades.
I'd tell the co-op we keep using it for **quotes and design**.
think: I think the **heat pump boom** carries my job either way.
I think my job is about as **safe** as junior work gets.
do: Finish my **licence next year**, then the battery storage certificate.
Keep using **AI to study** the wiring rules.
feel: I feel **calm**, and a little flat because I was excited.
S0.quote: The heat pump boom doesn't care whether AI is hype, because people still want lower bills.
fieldNote: Erik's work rides the **energy transition**, which doesn't depend on AI.
He uses AI as a **private tutor** for questions he's too shy to ask.
He credits his partner Theo for the **savings habit**.

steps.text: Finish the electrician's licence next year
Take the battery storage certificate after the licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one sounds like where things are going anyway. And honestly it might be good for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op is well placed and so are the trades. I'd also say loudly that office workers being dropped need a real safety net, because I'm not going to cheer while Theo's friends lose jobs. I'd post about a shorter working week too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the design and quoting side of our work speeds up, which means more jobs for the people doing the fitting. If AI does the heat pump design in ten minutes, the co-op can say yes to three times as many houses, and someone still has to climb onto the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI design tools at the co-op, since I'm the one who uses them every day. I'd push in the co-op meeting to hire another apprentice with the extra work. I'd keep studying for the licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a guilty edge because other people would be hurting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Whose job are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo's sister Clara, who does bookings for a travel company. She's already been told the team's moving to a chatbot. She'd laugh at me being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you suggest she come into the trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her about the co-op's apprenticeship, yes. She's practical, she built her own shelves. But she's 34, and starting on apprentice pay at 34 is hard, I know that.

say: I'd say the **trades are well placed**, and so is the co-op.
I'd demand a real **safety net** for office workers.
think: I think faster design means **more fitting jobs** for us.
I think someone still has to **climb onto the roof**.
do: Set up **AI design tools** at the co-op.
Push the co-op to **hire an apprentice** with the extra work.
feel: I feel **excited**, with a guilty edge for those hurting.
S1.quote: If AI does the heat pump design in ten minutes, the co-op can say yes to three times as many houses, and someone still has to climb onto the roof.
fieldNote: Erik expects **more work** for fitters as design gets cheaper.
His guilt is concrete: **Clara**, Theo's sister, is losing her bookings job.
He'd use the **co-op's structure** to share the gains.

steps.text: Set up AI heat pump design tools for the co-op
Propose hiring another apprentice at the co-op meeting
Keep studying for the licence each evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow, okay. Thinking AI in 2028, robots in 2031. That's fast enough to make my stomach turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public plan right now, a wealth tax on the AI firms and a guaranteed income. I'd be posting a lot, probably too much. At the co-op I'd say worker ownership is how we survive this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my edge, knowing the tools, disappears in two years because the tools don't need me to explain them. The robots get to me three years after the thinking AI, and three years is exactly how long it takes me to stop being a junior. So I'd only just be good when it stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn everything about installing and maintaining the robots, because someone has to. I'd push the co-op to buy one early, as a group, so we own it instead of a big firm. I'd raise savings to 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be moving, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The co-op buying a robot early. Where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan from the co-op bank, plus each of us putting in a share, maybe 1,000 each. That's a big chunk of my savings. But I'd rather own a piece of the robot than compete with someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Theo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teaching's probably safer than my job now, which is a strange sentence. Then we'd talk about whether to have kids later than we planned. We'd probably wait.

say: I'd call for a **wealth tax** on AI firms and a guaranteed income.
I'd say **worker ownership** is how the co-op survives.
think: I think my **edge with tools** disappears within two years.
I'd only just stop being **a junior** when robots arrive.
do: Learn to **install and maintain** the robots.
Push the co-op to **buy a robot** early, as a group.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: The robots get to me three years after the thinking AI, and three years is exactly how long it takes me to stop being a junior.
fieldNote: Erik spots the cruel timing: robots arrive just as he **stops being junior**.
He'd put **1,000** into a robot share rather than compete with one.
He'd push back **having children** with Theo.

steps.text: Put 1,000 into a co-op share to buy an install robot
Learn to service and program install robots
Delay plans for children with Theo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's better. That's time to get somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, a public plan and a tax, just with less shouting. I'd say the co-op can be a model for how trades handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get my licence, get good, and then become the person at the co-op who runs the machines and checks the work. I'd rather be the electrician who signs off a robot's wiring than the last human still drilling holes in roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence, the battery certificate, then a course in commissioning, which is checking systems work properly before handover. I'd keep using AI daily and start using it on design jobs at the co-op. Savings stay at 200.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I guess. It's a lot of change, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check the robot's work. What if the robots check their own work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then somebody has to be legally on the hook, and the law changes slowly. I'd bet on that for a while. If I'm wrong, I'd go into training people, or the co-op's management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, who's 61 and does only roof mounting. She'd be retiring around then anyway, but she needs those last years of pay. I'd want the co-op to keep her on even if she's slower than the robot.

say: I'd repeat the call for a **public plan and tax**, more calmly.
I'd hold up the **co-op as a model** for the trades.
think: I think I can become the one who **runs the machines**.
I'd rather **sign off** robot wiring than be the last driller.
do: Take the licence, battery certificate, then a **commissioning course**.
Use **AI on design** jobs at the co-op.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but like I'm steering.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the electrician who signs off a robot's wiring than the last human still drilling holes in roofs.
fieldNote: Erik bets on **legal responsibility** staying human for a while.
He has a **fallback** in training or co-op management.
He'd protect **Ruth**, 61, through her last working years.

steps.text: Take a commissioning course after the battery certificate
Use AI design tools on co-op jobs weekly
Argue at the co-op to keep Ruth on until she retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right, if we start now. I'd talk about it at the co-op and online as an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think with ten years I'd end up somewhere good, maybe as a partner in the co-op running a team. A ten-year warning is enough time to turn a nervous junior into the person who decides which robots the co-op buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my licence, then master electrician over the next six years, and start learning how the co-op is run. I'd use AI daily, obviously. And we'd go ahead with plans for kids in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm in the slow ones, anxious in the fast one. What's the biggest difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to stop being a junior. In two years I'm still mounting isolators upside down. In ten, I'm the one who knows what good looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would make the ten-year version go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big firms got the robots first and undercut every small co-op. Then I'd be working for them on their terms. That's why I'd push the policy stuff even in the slow version.

say: I'd say this is the version we can **get right**.
I'd call it an **opportunity** at the co-op and online.
think: I think I could become a **co-op partner** running a team.
I'd be the one deciding which **robots the co-op buys**.
do: Take the licence, then **master electrician** within six years.
feel: I feel **calm**, even a bit hopeful.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is enough time to turn a nervous junior into the person who decides which robots the co-op buys.
fieldNote: Erik's mood depends on **time** to stop being junior.
His real fear is **big firms** getting robots first and undercutting co-ops.
He'd keep pushing **policy** even in the gentle version.

steps.text: Take the master electrician licence within six years
Join the co-op's management meetings to learn how it's run
Start trying for children with Theo in a few years
Lobby for rules that let small co-ops buy robots too

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only just stop being a junior when the robots came. What would help is letting small co-ops borrow cheaply to own robots, so the people who fit heat pumps own the machines that replace them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd stay in the trade at all. I would. I like roofs, even in winter, mostly.

headlineQuote: What would help is letting small co-ops borrow cheaply to own robots, so the people who fit heat pumps own the machines that replace them.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old junior** at a worker-owned solar and heat pump co-op.
He uses **AI daily** as a tutor and is excited by new tech.
He sees AI boosting **fitting work**, but fears robots arriving just as he gets good.
He'd answer with **shared ownership**: the co-op buying robots so workers own the machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive as he stops being a junior.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small co-ops to own robots themselves.
